title: Inflationary Bispectra and IR Physics from Quantum Simulators
abstract: Bose-Einstein condensates have been used successfully as quantum simulators for early-universe particle production. Here we extend this analogy to the interacting theory. To this end, we compute the leading interaction terms expected in a general experimental setup that determine the 3-point correlations. We apply them to cosmologically motivated expanding model universes, but also periodically oscillating ones. While expanding scale factors do not necessarily lead to easily observable signatures due to experimental constraints on the realizable scale factor, periodically driven ones produce resonant correlators that grow linearly over time and lend themselves well to experimental detection. One direct application of this analysis is the experimental study of late-time infrared divergencies often discussed in the context of massless scalars in de Sitter space.
summary: This paper uses Bose-Einstein condensates as quantum simulators to study interacting quantum field theories relevant to the early universe, specifically focusing on inflationary bispectra. By analyzing the system in various time-dependent backgrounds, the authors demonstrate that periodic driving can induce resonant growth in correlation functions, offering a pathway for experimental detection of cosmological signatures.
main_problem: The paper extends the use of Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs) as quantum simulators from free theory phenomena to study interacting theories relevant to early-universe physics, such as inflation.
main_result: The analysis shows that while expanding scale factors lead to expected IR divergences, periodically driven backgrounds can produce resonant correlators that grow linearly and are potentially detectable in experiments.
method: The authors derive interaction terms mimicking Effective Field Theory (EFT) of inflation and apply quantum field theory techniques (Schwinger-Keldysh formalism) to calculate 3-point correlations (bispectra) in time-dependent backgrounds.
model_or_system: The system is a BEC of a cold atom gas, modeled as a relativistic scalar field $\Phi$ in a time-dependent Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker (FLRW) background. The analysis focuses on the phase fluctuations ($\phi$) of the condensate.
key_observables: Momentum space 3-point function (bispectrum) of density and phase fluctuations, and the resonant growth of correlators.
important_parameters: The dimensionless coupling $\kappa$, the scale factor $a(t)$ (especially periodic/triangle wave profiles), and the resonance condition defined by the ratio $a_{\max}/a_{\min}$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the BEC is very large, boundary effects are negligible, and approximations are made when solving the mode equations for different scale factor regimes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the scale factor $a(t)$ interpolating between different regimes and visualize resonant conditions in the short wavelength regime, showing clear resonant bands.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from deriving the effective action for the BEC phase fluctuations, to establishing the formalism for calculating correlators in an FLRW background, and finally analyzing the mode functions and bispectra in specific cosmological regimes (accelerating, decelerating, and periodic).
why_interesting: This work directly bridges the gap between fundamental condensed matter systems (BECs) and high-energy cosmology (inflation/de Sitter space), providing a concrete, experimentally accessible platform to test complex quantum field theory predictions.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Scale factor a(t) as a function of time. The experiment is set up at time t0. Between the times ti and tf, the scale factor is continuously interpolating the values ai and af. The correlation function is then measured at time tm, when the scale factor has been held at a constant value for some time. This figure is inspired by [26].

Figure 2: Density bispectrum Bρ. a) and b): As a function of k1 and k2 at fixed k3 = 1.0 and fixed ti = 1, for two different γ. We plot the absolute value which makes the patterns easier to read off, but both positive and negative values can be reached. Shown are multiple parameters in a 30×30 grid, while the k1 and k2 axes are shared. The triangles in the corners mark the kinematically excluded regions ka + kb < kc for {a, b, c} = {1, 2, 3}. The columns show different tf, while the rows in each block show different wait times ∆tm = tm −tf, as indicated above each row. Larger tf usually lead to larger values, and larger ∆tm lead to a interference-like redistribution of the values. γ = 1.1...

Figure 3: Phase bispectrum BS. The general structure of this figure is the same as for figure 2. a): As a function of k1 and k2 at fixed k3 = 1.0. Similarly to Bρ, the overall size of the values is growing with tf, while larger ∆tm lead to stronger patterns. Again, larger γ lead to larger values overall. b): Late-time behavior at k1 = k2 = k3 = 0.2 at different γ as a function of final time t = tf = tm. Values γ < 1 lead to oscillations and γ > 1 lead to growth, which matches the dependence on tf from table 1 qualitatively. Since the growth is linear and not quartic, larger values can be reached at earlier times than for Bρ.

Figure 4: Periodic scale factor a(t) as a function of time. The experiment is set up at time t0 with a scale factor of a(t0) = amin. Between the times ti and tf, the scale factor is continuously oscillating between the values amin and amax. The correlation function then is measured at time tm, when the scale factor has been held at a constant value amin for some time.
